title: There's No Free Lunch: Risk and Return
subtitle: Anyone promising high returns with no risk is lying or confused. Understand the trade-off and you'll never fall for it.
hook: If an investment offered guaranteed 20% a year with zero risk, everyone would pour money in until the return got competed down to boring. That never-quite-happens is the deepest law of markets: **you only get higher expected returns by taking more risk.** No exceptions that last. Today: what 'risk' actually means, and why the promise of high-return-no-risk is always a red flag.

builds_on.label: Putting a Price on the Future

sections.heading: Risk = how much it can swing
sections.body:
In finance, 'risk' mostly means **volatility** — how much an investment's value bounces around. A savings account barely moves (low risk, low return). Stocks lurch up and down (higher risk) and, *on average over long periods*, pay more to compensate you for the stomach-churning ride.

Why the link? Because investors dislike uncertainty. To get people to hold a bumpy asset, it has to dangle a higher expected reward — the **risk premium**. Remove the premium and nobody holds the risky thing.

sections.caption: The risk–return line: safer assets sit low-left, riskier ones climb up-right. You move up the reward axis only by moving right on risk.

sections.label: The scam detector
sections.body: "High returns, guaranteed, no risk" is the signature of a fraud (see: every Ponzi scheme). Real high returns come with real chances of loss. If someone has genuinely found risk-free excess return, they don't need your money — and the market would erase it fast anyway.

sections.label: Risk ≠ ruin, though
sections.body: Volatility isn't the only risk. The one that actually matters is **permanent loss** — being forced to sell at the bottom, or an asset going to zero. A bumpy asset you can hold for 20 years may be *less* risky for you than a 'stable' one that quietly erodes to inflation. Match the risk to your time horizon and your ability to not panic.

sections.caption: Risk vs. return for beginners — why they're two sides of the same coin.

takeaways: Higher **expected** return requires taking more **risk** — the risk premium.
'Risk' usually means **volatility** (how much value swings), but the real danger is **permanent loss**.
Cash < bonds < stocks < speculation, roughly, on the risk–return line.
'High return, no risk, guaranteed' = a red flag for fraud, every time.
The right risk level depends on your **time horizon** and your nerve.

quiz.q: Why do riskier assets tend to offer higher expected returns?
options: They must dangle a 'risk premium' to get anyone to hold the uncertainty
quiz.explain: Investors dislike uncertainty, so a bumpy asset must pay more to be held.

quiz.q: Someone offers 'guaranteed 15%/yr, zero risk.' Best response?
options: Treat it as a red flag — risk-free excess return doesn't persist
quiz.explain: That combination is the calling card of Ponzi schemes. Real reward comes with real risk.

quiz.q: BOSS: A retiree needs the money next year; a 25-year-old won't touch it for 30 years. Who can rationally hold more volatile stocks?
options: The 25-year-old — a long horizon lets short-term swings average out
quiz.explain: Volatility hurts most when you're forced to sell soon. Time horizon changes what 'risky' means for you.

tg_quiz.q: "Guaranteed 15% a year, zero risk" — what is it?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — risk-free excess return doesn't last. Classic scam signal.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's a red flag — real returns come with real risk.
tg_quiz.explain: No free lunch: reward requires risk.
